meta.title: Who really said "Go for a business that any idiot can run, because sooner or later any idiot probably is going to be running it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Buffett. Peter Lynch wrote it in One Up On Wall Street (1989); Buffett used the adage in 2008 but credited “they.” Quote Investigator traces it to Lynch.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Go for a business that any idiot can run, because sooner or later any idiot probably is going to be running it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Buffett — Peter Lynch, in One Up On Wall Street (1989). Buffett repeated the adage in 2008 and credited it to “they.” Wikiquote calls the Buffett version misattributed.

answer.label: Not Warren Buffett — actually Peter Lynch
answer.authorDates: Born 1944 · American investor who ran Fidelity’s Magellan Fund, 1977–1990
answer.sourceLine: The line is Peter Lynch’s, from his 1989 bestseller One Up On Wall Street, where he wrote that when somebody says any idiot could run a business, “that’s a plus as far as I’m concerned.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the compact wording that circulates today to Lynch in USA Today on 7 March 1989 — and notes that when Buffett used the idea in 2008 he credited it vaguely to “they,” not to himself.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: <cite>USA Today</cite>, 7 March 1989, p. 4B (as cited by Quote Investigator)

source.excerpt: When somebody says, ‘Any idiot could run this joint,’ that’s a plus as far as I’m concerned, because sooner or later any idiot probably is going to be running it.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ answered a reader who had met the idea in a 2008 Buffett interview: Buffett “was not asserting originality” and credited it to “they,” while Lynch had put it in print in 1989. QI cites the book as chapter 8 of the Simon and Schuster edition, text checked against the First Fireside Edition, 2000, p. 130.
QI also cites the compact wording to “Track Companies, Not Markets,” USA Today, 7 March 1989, p. 4B — the form that matches how the line is quoted today. See the QI write-up ↗.
Wikiquote’s Peter Lynch page ↗ carries the book sentence sourced to One Up On Wall Street (1989), while its Buffett page ↗ lists a Buffett-worded version under Misattributed and points to Lynch.
The Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ confirms the edition details: One up on Wall Street, Peter Lynch, New York: Simon and Schuster, 1989, 318 pages, ISBN 0671661035.
source.excerptNote: That is the book form. The tighter sentence people quote today — “Go for a business that any idiot can run…” — is the version Lynch gave USA Today in March 1989, which is why the two wordings differ slightly. Both are cited to Lynch by Quote Investigator ↗.

author.name: Peter Lynch
author.heading: Who Peter Lynch was
author.metaLine: Born 1944 · American investor, fund manager & author
author.bio: Peter Lynch managed Fidelity’s Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, posting a 29.2% average annual return and growing the fund from about $18 million to $14 billion — the record that made him one of the most-quoted investors alive. In 1989 he distilled his method into One Up On Wall Street, written with John Rothchild, which argued that ordinary investors can beat professionals by noticing good companies before Wall Street does. The book sold more than a million copies, which is exactly why its best one-liners escaped into circulation and started getting pinned on more famous names.

cite.sourceCitation: Peter Lynch with John Rothchild, One Up On Wall Street (New York: Simon and Schuster, 1989), chap. 8 — text checked by Quote Investigator against the First Fireside Edition, 2000, p. 130. misattribution.heading: The Buffett problem
misattribution.intro: This is an investing adage with a documented author who is not the famous name attached to it. Buffett never claimed it — the credit was handed to him by other people.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Buffett page ↗ lists a Buffett-worded version of the adage in its Misattributed section, with the note that while Buffett is fond of repeating it, he also often credits Peter Lynch.

In a 20 May 2008 Associated Press story, per Quote Investigator ↗, Buffett introduced the idea as something “they say in the stock market” — explicitly attributing it to an unnamed source rather than himself.

items.scope: Buffett’s own version of the thought
items.why: Speaking to the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission in May 2010, Buffett said a really good business is one “your idiot nephew could run,” as reported by Yahoo Finance ↗ in March 2016 — his own phrasing, and not the sentence quoted here.
Lynch put it in print in One Up On Wall Street, and the compact wording appears under his name in USA Today on 7 March 1989, both cited by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Peter Lynch wrote it in 1989; Buffett borrowed the thought and said so. Quote Investigator’s findings ↗.

context.heading: Why the idea stuck
lead: Lynch’s point was not a joke about executives — it was a screening rule. His 1989 book ↗ sorts companies into six types and argues that an ordinary investor’s edge lies in simple, understandable businesses spotted before Wall Street notices them. A business whose success does not depend on a genius at the top is a business whose success you can actually predict.

The saying then did what good sayings do: it detached from its author. Buffett has used the same thought more than once — in a May 2008 Associated Press story he framed it as something “they say in the stock market,” per Quote Investigator ↗ — and because he is the more famous investor, the line drifted onto his name.
context.detailsSummary: How the credit slipped from Lynch to Buffett
detailsBody: The question that prompted Quote Investigator’s 2010 investigation came from a reader who had encountered the idea in a 2008 Buffett interview and thought it sounded familiar. QI’s answer was that the reader had probably met Lynch’s version first — Buffett was passing along an adage, not coining one.

Buffett kept returning to the same test in his own words. A March 2016 Yahoo Finance piece ↗ quotes him, from a May 2010 interview with the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, saying of a genuinely good business that “your idiot nephew could run it” — and that article itself points readers to Lynch for the more famous formulation.
context.pull: Buffett said “they say.” Lynch was the “they.”
